request: Filing a bug report but I haven't filled in any details yet — no React version, no reproduction steps, no code example, and no description of current or expected behavior.

On a hosted database project, creating a webhook fails with a schema-not-found error even though the required extension is already enabled. The same failure shows up in a freshly created project set up with just a small sample table and one simple function handler. Could the underlying schema be reprovisioned so webhook creation works again as expected?

The Terraform release downloads page returns a 504 Gateway Timeout whenever I try to open it, while other pages on the same host load fine. Is this a known outage on the hosted release infrastructure, since nothing shows up on the usual status page?
This report's title is only a phone number, with a link to a spot in the TypeScript standard library type definitions and no explanation of what problem or request it's about.

Ask whether there is a way to change the email address and login for a hosted database account to a new address, without losing existing tables and database setup; the expectation is that the data and configuration survive the change.
A bug report was submitted using an empty issue template, with a nonsensical title and no repro steps, version, or description filled in. There isn't enough here to act on.

On my hosted project, I deleted database rows directly with SQL instead of going through the storage API, which left the underlying files behind in the bucket. The API and dashboard now show nothing for those rows, but the storage usage graph hasn't dropped, and I have no way to purge the leftover files myself. Can the platform team clear the orphaned objects so usage reflects reality?

A submitted bug report has no coherent description of an actual problem, just fragments of system and GPU information with no explanation of what fails or what's expected. There's nothing actionable to investigate. Please confirm whether there's a real defect here at all.

The cloud project dashboard gets stuck in an infinite loading loop every time I open it, even after clearing cookies and cache, trying a private window, disabling extensions, switching networks, and forcing a fresh login. I expected it to load normally instead of hanging indefinitely. Is this a server-side problem, since local troubleshooting is exhausted and the in-app support form can't be reached while the dashboard itself is unusable?
This report consists of a large block of unrelated server code pasted in, with no explanation of how it relates to Node.js or what change is being asked for.

Ask how to build a custom plugin that generates utility classes dynamically from a set of JSON design tokens, and what API pattern is recommended so the generated utilities don't bloat the final compiled stylesheet.

How do I make a gomobile build reproducible? I want to lock the mobile SDKs, Java, and the gomobile and gobind tool versions, but gomobile init keeps fetching the latest gobind on its own rather than using a version pinned in the module files. Would merging the two command-line tools into one binary fix that?

The has-* variant works for me when styling an element based on a matching child element, but I can't get the same pattern to match a data attribute on that child instead. Is targeting a data attribute with has-* actually supported, and if so what's the right syntax?

Someone is asking how to correctly use a particular library feature in a production environment, without specifying which feature they mean. Please clarify what they need and point them to the relevant documentation.
How should JWT authentication for protected routes be implemented in a Next.js application built on the App Router? Looking for the currently recommended pattern rather than a workaround.
How do I use the Tailwind CSS Vite plugin together with Vite version 8?

Ask for help after upgrading a package manager to a new major version: reinstalling it, clearing caches, and pinning the version in the manifest still leaves the content-addressable store reporting the prior major version. The answer is likely already covered in the documentation.

With pnpm's newer runtime command replacing the older env command, what's the right way now to list which Node versions are installed locally, and which ones are available remotely? The previous remote-listing option doesn't seem to have a direct replacement.

During a production build of my App Router project, a server component that's several layers deep in the tree reads request headers or cookies, and that causes static generation to abort with a dynamic-server-usage error. Wrapping that component tree in a custom boundary didn't stop the static worker from failing during evaluation. There's probably a documented way to opt a route like this out of static generation that I'm missing — what is it?

After deploying an app to a hosting platform, an environment variable that works locally comes back undefined at runtime in production. The expectation is that it should resolve the same way after deployment. Can you explain the correct way to configure environment variables for that platform, ideally pointing to the relevant documentation?

For a type assertion function typed with a predicate, does the predicate need to hold true in both directions, or is it acceptable for it to be true only one way? Trying to confirm the intended semantics before relying on this pattern.

Can several pnpm install processes safely run at the same time across different projects that share one content-addressable store, without one process's writes interfering with or corrupting another's?
Ask what compatibility standard or authoritative source a type checker follows when deciding which web platform APIs it should ship type definitions for.

Vite 8 has been released, but the Tailwind Vite plugin still declares a peer dependency range that stops before Vite 8, so installing now prints a peer dependency warning. Is there a plan to widen that range to support Vite 8?

I found a site that looks like an unofficial mirror of the Chinese Node.js docs, but I can't find any announcement confirming it's authorized. Is this mirror actually supported by the project, and is it safe to download from?

A styling plugin spaces paragraphs and similar elements using margins rather than padding. Is there a specific reason margins were chosen over padding, and is there a supported way to reconfigure the plugin to use padding instead?

Why does the project's public website display a Chinese ICP filing registration number even though the site doesn't appear to be hosted in, or served through, mainland China? Looking for the technical or legal reason behind that filing.
Why did pnpm add support for managing Rust and Python packages? I can't find any discussion of this in the implementation work, and I'm not against it, just curious about the reasoning.
Ask whether there are plans to publish a container image for a package manager that also bundles a JavaScript runtime, instead of requiring the runtime to be installed separately.

I'm curious why Chrome isn't generally recommended for use with screen readers, and whether that could become more of a problem for accessibility going forward. Just looking for background on the reasoning, not reporting a bug.

When a role that declares private role variables is used as a dependency more than once, those private vars stop taking effect, unlike when the role is only included a single time. I can reproduce this with a role listed as a dependency twice with different vars each time, but I don't have exact version or environment details to share right now.

When building an app with a bundler, a proxy/middleware file with no import relationship to a database client library still ends up with unrelated native binaries in its generated file-trace, seen by running a production build and inspecting the trace output. The reproduction lives in a private repo, so no public example is included yet, though one could be built if useful. Investigate why this happens.

After the Turbopack dev server runs for a long time under continuous activity, such as repeated page requests, file-triggered recompiles, and long-lived client connections, it eventually crashes with a RangeError about a Map exceeding its maximum size inside an internal async hook. There's no minimal reproduction yet since it only shows up after an extended session on a large app; filing the crash details in case they help narrow down the cause.

On Windows, the Turbopack dev server spawns an unbounded number of Node worker processes and eventually exhausts all memory, seen with a large pnpm monorepo using the App Router and standalone output. I can't share a minimal reproduction because every attempt crashes my workstation within minutes, but I can run diagnostics against the real project.

Report that after upgrading a primary application zone while an older secondary zone version stays in place, the secondary zone starts returning a redirect-loop error, but only in the hosted production environment, not locally; it worked correctly before the primary zone's upgrade, and no reproduction steps have been provided yet.

ViewTransition doesn't appear to work correctly in a right-to-left layout: the animation debug panel shows a transition running, but nothing changes visually on screen. No specific steps or version are given beyond that.

This bundled several small leftover items found during a mass-merge sweep: a wording defect, a missed type check, two possible conflicts, a wrong commit subject line, and a design change needing review. Since filing it, all of those turned out already resolved elsewhere except one — a skill file's line-count limit is sitting exactly at its cap with no headroom, which is still worth checking against the current tree.

On the project's public site, a hidden display mode shows a small attribution line that wraps onto two lines on one page but stays on one line on another. Steps: enable the display mode, then compare the attribution text between the two pages. Since this depends on the live site's current content, the specific pages compared may no longer match what's described.

An open design question asks whether a configuration flag that disables a research-summary requirement is a full opt-out for its validation gate, or only suppresses one rule inside it. The filer notes the decision this was based on had already been settled days and many merged changes earlier, so the premise may be out of date. If still genuinely unsettled against current code, raise it again fresh.

In ReactDOMRoot.js there's a small comment typo: 'untill' should read 'until'. The surrounding comment describes a workaround for concurrent features that may already be stabilized, so the note itself might no longer be accurate.

Report that a resize control on a third-party scheduling demo cannot be operated by keyboard, blocking keyboard and screen-reader users from resizing panels. Reproduce by opening the demo page and trying to reach the control using only the keyboard. Note the report may no longer reflect the demo's current state since it was filed a while ago.

The documentation explains what a hydration mismatch is but doesn't give a practical walkthrough for debugging one in a real server-rendered app. Please add a guide covering how to figure out what caused a mismatch, which component is responsible, and how to resolve it step by step.

React DevTools' component inspector sometimes locks up when a selected component is re-rendering rapidly, for example due to polling or animation-driven updates. To reproduce: watch a frequently re-rendering component in the tree view and select it — the panel becomes unresponsive until you switch tabs or pick a different component. I haven't retested this in a while, so it may no longer reproduce on the current version.

When a debug-channel option is enabled on the streaming client, an element inside a lazily-loaded chunk stops being recognized as valid, though it passes with the option off. A standalone reproduction confirms this using a short delay simulating a separate debug transport. The tested builds are pinned to past pre-release snapshots that may already be outdated.

When a lazily loaded component is wrapped in a Suspense boundary with a fallback spinner, the fallback re-renders several times while the network response is artificially delayed by a few seconds, causing visible flicker, especially on slower devices. It should instead render once and stay stable until the lazy component resolves. This was filed without confirming it still reproduces on a current build, so the premise may already be stale.

Compiling a short snippet that causes a constant overflow triggers an internal compiler error: a panic with an assertion failure inside the compiler's type-recording code, with a full crash stack trace attached. This was found automatically by a fuzzing tool rather than filed by a person.

Report, filed automatically by a collector tool, that a SIMD-related compiler test consistently fails during continuous integration; a build log and an internal compiler error with a stack trace are attached, and it reproduces by running the architecture-specific SIMD test suite for that package.

A fuzzing tool triggered an internal compiler crash: the compiler panics with an '!on_stack' assertion failure inside the code generation backend while compiling with several unstable flags enabled. A crash log and the exact command that triggers it are attached.

The TypeScript Playground doesn't expose the resolveJsonModule compiler option, which is blocking me from filing a repro that depends on it. Should the Playground start supporting this option specifically, or open up arbitrary tsconfig options in general? A decision on scope is needed before implementing either.

The project's initializer writes many text files into a new repository but ships no line-ending configuration for them. On one operating system, a single edit can convert every line ending in a file to a different style at the storage level, making a diff-based review step useless since the whole file appears changed. Should the initializer start shipping an explicit line-ending policy, and what should it declare?

Proposes a new command that would write a second file to disk capturing the actual live state of resources, similar to how planning polls infrastructure, with secrets redacted, so drift caused by manual out-of-band changes is easy to see in version control. Should this ship as a first-class subcommand, and if so, what should the redaction and output behavior look like?

Add support for replicating Azure NetApp Files volumes across availability zones within the same region; the existing module only supports replication across regions. Should this be added, and if so, how should it sit alongside the existing cross-region option?

Propose adding a manual page for the free-threading build of the interpreter, which currently has none. Ask the maintainers to decide whether to add one before any change is made; a likely fix would be a small build-script adjustment to use the correct version variable.

AWS has released a simplified CLI-based login authentication flow, and the S3 backend should support using it instead of the existing credential methods. Supporting it would need an updated version of the AWS SDK dependency the backend already relies on. Should this be added, and if so how should it fit alongside the existing S3 backend authentication options?

Teams that switched on AWS Inspector manually through the console or CLI have no path to bring that setup under Terraform without deleting and recreating it. Add terraform import support for the Inspector enabler resource, or explain why it can't be supported, so we know whether to plan around a rebuild instead.

As a security engineer, I'd like the infrastructure-as-code tool to support configuring the lowest allowed inbound TLS cipher suite for an App Service resource on Azure, so deployments can be restricted to cipher suites approved by internal policy. There's currently no way to configure this through the provider. Should a new setting be added, and what should it be called?

Requests official support for building and running the tool on an old, no-longer-supported version of Windows, noting the filer has already produced working binaries by patching the toolchain themselves. Should the project take on maintaining a build target for that unsupported operating system, or is this out of scope?

Add support for post-quantum TLS key exchange, such as X25519MLKEM768, for remote-state HTTPS connections and as a general primitive providers can use, since the underlying Go runtime already supports it from a recent version. Should this be adopted, and would it require raising the minimum required Go version?

Ask the maintainers to decide, before any implementation begins, what should happen to a validator warning that flags an overly long business-rule cell: keep it, remove it entirely, or narrow when it triggers so splitting the rule isn't the only fix it suggests. Note that removing or narrowing it could break specs that currently trip the warning.

The DNS message parser correctly rejects malformed names, but callers cannot reliably tell a proven parsing error apart from one caused by truncated input. A proposed API addition would let a caller suppress that diagnostic when data is merely missing, while still raising it when bytes already prove a real error; it wouldn't change which messages get accepted. Should this be adopted? It needs review through the external proposal process.

For the demonstrated-failure check, we need to decide where an observed failure gets recorded, since the scoring checklist only counts failures that have a place to point to. Options: cite the observation in a test-case row so it's scored, log it as a formal change against the specification, or add it as a new decision entry. I'd lean toward the test-case row citation, but this needs a decision before implementing.

Proposal: change a standard-library error-construction function from a plain function into a swappable function variable, so it can optionally be intercepted at runtime to attach stack traces or other enrichment, without altering default behavior or breaking existing callers. This would go through the formal proposal process for review before any change lands.

Proposes adding a new pure-Go, allocation-free 3D triangle rasterizer package to the extended image library, covering use cases like headless validation of 3D assets, automated thumbnail generation, and terminal graphics where GPU drivers aren't available. This needs review and a decision from the language's public proposal process before any implementation, tests, or documented contract work begins.

Proposal: replace the confusing 'as const' syntax with a new 'valueof' operator. Should the team accept a new keyword to address this confusion, given it touches core type syntax and needs to go through the language's own proposal review process?

Ask the maintainers to decide, before stabilizing a compiler flag that sets environment variables, how it should interact with the compiler's own tool search: never affect it, always affect it, only affect it case by case, or apply only to environment lookups inside the compiled program itself.

The documented way to advance a synctest bubble's clock to an exact time can silently land on the wrong instant when that time is already past, because the sleep call returns immediately with no error. The proposal adds a dedicated sleep-until function with guards turning that silent misuse into a panic, so a mistimed test fails loudly instead of quietly passing. Should this be adopted? It needs review through the external proposal process.

Proposal: add a replacement package for the existing URL-handling package because its name collides with the natural variable name for a URL value. Copy its files under the new name, deprecate the old package with aliases and an automatic-fix hint, and phase the migration over two releases so existing code keeps working. This changes standard-library surface, so it needs sign-off from the language proposal process first.

Proposal: when encoding nested struct fields to JSON with a custom-marshaler option, the marshaler applies to the top-level struct but not to nested node types within its fields. Working around this currently requires manually reflecting over each struct's fields. Could an API be added so a custom marshaler applies recursively to nested fields? This is going through the formal proposal review process.

A batch of review findings from an earlier merged pull request were never answered before it landed, and each one needs re-checking against the current codebase since the review round has since moved on. The findings bundle several unrelated kinds of problems together, including at least one about a spec's execution ledger needing repair, so they should be split apart and re-triaged individually rather than handled as one item.

A previous change merged with several review comments left unanswered; none were addressed before merging, so each still needs to be checked against the current codebase. This bundles several separate, unrelated follow-up items together at different priority levels.

Report that of the project's open pull requests surveyed, nine need attention: most have failing continuous-integration jobs such as unit tests or a version-floor check, two have no failing job but unresolved review comments, and one has no CI run triggered at all. This bundles several independent, differently-shaped problems and asks for each to be reviewed again.

Several review findings from a recently merged change were never answered before it merged, and now need to be checked again against the current codebase. They cover different kinds of concerns - reordering options in an open change proposal, scheduling a follow-up, and other unrelated points - so each should be evaluated on its own rather than as a single item.

When a recent pull request merged, seven review-thread comments on it were never answered, covering a mix of different kinds of findings — some about handling an unreachable state as a defect, others about process and documentation details. None of them were checked against the code that's now on the main branch. Please re-triage each finding against the current main and note whether it still applies.

One top-level guidance file states a general rule against local tracking identifiers in source and Markdown files, but the fuller version of that rule carries an exemption for changelog entries that the summary leaves out. Since a changelog is itself Markdown, relying on the short summary makes every changelog entry look like a violation of a rule never meant to cover it. The summary should be corrected to keep the exemption.

The validation command never reads the reviewer's deliverable file that a documented completion gate is supposed to check, so it accepts a run whether that file is well-formed, malformed, or missing. Reproducible with a project whose reviewer file and top-level record are both valid: the check still reports zero errors. The gate exists in name only, since nothing in the code path reads the file it claims to enforce.

Two of the project's own rules contradict each other: one forbids referencing lower-layer identifiers or per-item details in certain policy files, while another requires exactly that kind of reference in a required table column there. Following both at once is impossible for any populated table; a maintainer needs to decide which rule gives way so that a compliant file becomes possible again.

Report that a node-status field recording a volume's attached device path is defined only in unix block-device terms, while the code assuming a unix-style device node causes undefined behavior for a different operating system's nodes. Expect a documented, platform-aware contract for the field and a fix to the code paths that wrongly assume a unix device node.

A config option meant to control which files get excluded when generating a role skeleton is parsed correctly and shows up in the config dump, but has no actual effect: matching files still get copied regardless of the setting. The option needs to actually be applied during the copy step so matching files are skipped as documented.

Two reference documents describing what to do when a per-item verification checkpoint fails disagree with each other: one says stay in the current state, fix it, and re-run; the other says switch to an exception state, put together a written decision record, and start a fresh tracking entry. Neither mentions the other's rule. We need a decision on which remedy is correct so the wrong document can be fixed.

A policy document restates inline the full list of fields a parallel worker must return, describing it as covering every field, but it only names eleven of the twenty-three fields the authoritative contract defines. Because of that gap, an otherwise correct worker block fails validation against one of the twelve omitted fields. The inline list should be corrected to match the contract, or replaced with a reference to it.

The acceptance-test scanner builds its file-matching patterns from a hardcoded list covering only a couple of programming languages, and never reads the project's own configured test-file patterns. In a repository written in any other language it matches zero test files, so the coverage gate can never see anything as covered, and ends up simultaneously impossible to pass and not actually protective, all without raising an error.

There's no way to record that a screen intentionally used nothing from outside sources, so a manifest that was never written looks the same as one stating that nothing was reused. The check only validates a manifest when one is present, so an omitted one silently passes either way; there should be an explicit way to say nothing was procured.

Report that one workflow skill's role list declares and routes an agent whose stated mission is exactly what that same skill's own non-goals forbid it from doing, with nothing in the skill reconciling the contradiction. Ask the maintainers to decide how to resolve it before anything is changed.

The acceptance-test validation profile is supposed to run every check the acceptance workflow depends on, but it skips the one that catches placeholder test stubs. As a result, a test written as a stub rather than a real assertion can pass that gate silently, with the gap only caught by a different, unrelated profile. The missing check needs to run under the acceptance profile too.

Under the experimental mutation-restriction feature, code should get a compiler error when it constructs a restricted struct directly with its positional (tuple-style) constructor from outside the module that owns it, but right now no error is raised. The simplest fix is probably to reject any case where the compiler-generated constructor is used as an expression at all.

A validation run figures out which checks it skipped by consulting a manually maintained table that maps code-family prefixes to gate groups, covering twelve entries across twenty-five patterns. The module producing design-validation results emits twelve additional code families absent from the table under any group, so a partial run understates its own skip set. The table needs to be extended or generated to account for every emitted family.

When every acceptance test on a spec sits at a low enough level to be exempt from a coverage obligation, that spec is silently excluded from the check with nothing flagging it. A summary does list exempt test cases, but only as one combined count project-wide, with no per-spec breakdown, so a green result can look like full coverage even though roughly three-quarters of one spec's obligations were never counted.

The traceability scan that counts acceptance-test coverage builds its own list of test files from fixed directories and only applies default exclusion patterns, so a project's own configured exclude patterns are never honored. Files a project explicitly excludes still get scanned and counted toward acceptance obligations.

Report that the automated check meant to verify a completed row's evidence section only confirms the section heading exists and checks nothing about its content, so an empty section, or one with fields naming a different row, is silently accepted with no findings. Reproduce by leaving a completed row's evidence section empty or filled with another row's fields, then running the validator.

A duplicate-identifier checker is supposed to catch the same identifier being declared twice, but it tracks duplicates by counting how many files contain an identifier rather than how many times it's declared inside a file. Two separate headings in the same file that both declare the same identifier go completely unreported, even though that's exactly the ambiguity the check exists to catch.

The command-line flag that sets the failure gate accepts a misspelled or unknown value without rejecting it, unlike its sibling enum flags which do validate and error on an unrecognized value. When that happens, the flag is silently treated as unset and the tool falls back to whatever the config file says, with no warning that the typo was ignored. Add the same validation the other flags already have.

A rule forbids internal capability identifiers above a threshold from appearing in shipped files, and three guard scripts enforce it with the same pattern requiring a leading zero. That pattern stops matching once the identifier reaches five digits without a leading zero, so once the counter passes that point, a forbidden identifier can slip past every guard. The shared pattern needs to keep matching beyond that boundary.

The completion gate checks each reviewer's approval field and its accompanying seal independently of one another, rather than confirming every reviewer's verdict for a given change actually comes from the same review round's evidence pack. A row could therefore pass even if its reviewer approvals were drawn from different, inconsistent review rounds, which the documented process assumes can never happen.

A finding raised after the main validation pass runs through a second, separate waiver check, but that check's verdicts are then discarded, so a waiver written against that finding is not honored and not rejected either, with nothing recorded to explain the gap. That disconnected second pass should be removed so late findings go through the same waiver handling as everything else.

Report that a named test suite exists in the codebase but is not run by any continuous-integration job, so it has no effect. Ask the maintainers to decide whether to add a job that runs it again, and if not, this asks that the suite be removed since it is no longer useful as is.

A template file was retired and the manifest now marks it as legacy, so new content shouldn't need to include it anymore. But the validator that used to require its presence, along with its error message and remediation text, is still active even though nothing else references it. Please remove the leftover validator, message, and remedy text for the retired file.

When an older family of validators was retired, one module was updated but six sibling modules were left disconnected from the validator runner and never removed. About two dozen rule IDs the changelog still advertises can now never fire, and a few of the dead modules even target filenames a separate active rule forbids outright. Please finish the retirement by deleting the disconnected modules and fixing the changelog to match.

A recorded timing artifact pins a test-file count for one project, but the codebase's current count has grown about nineteen percent above that figure, just under a twenty percent tolerance a related check allows before it's considered a different project. The pinned figure is close enough to that ceiling that a few more added files could break the check. It should be re-measured and updated before that happens.

Follow-up to an earlier accepted change that removed the lower bound on a prose-length check: the code now enforces only an upper limit, but two of the story-tree documents for one spec still state the old two-sided band as a requirement, across the requirement text, the business rules, the acceptance criteria, and an example. Those documents need to be brought back in line with what the code actually enforces now.

A shrink-only counter stored beside the data it tracks turned the main branch red for about forty minutes after two branches each changed the count independently, even though neither branch was actually wrong. One branch was cut before the counter existed, so its author had no way to know to update it; the count should be derived or reconciled automatically rather than hand-edited per branch.

Report that a specification's stated ceiling on the job instances a pull request touching only code may cost names a figure now less than half of what a complete run actually measures, because the CI lane set was later deliberately widened without updating the recorded ceiling. Ask for the stale figure to be brought in line with the current lane set.

An allowlist meant to hold only legacy exceptions to an English-only message rule has absorbed messages added well after that rule was already being enforced, so it no longer distinguishes genuinely old exceptions from ones that should never have been allowed onto the list. A batch of newer messages ended up added to the same list used to grandfather in the older ones.

A workflow phase is supposed to add one end-to-end test row per active story to each spec's test ledger, but none of the ledgers in this repository have been re-seeded since that phase's rules were written. Checking directly: in one pack, all nine stories are active and none has a matching row, so nine rows are silently missing. Please re-seed every ledger so a later pass doesn't add them unrecorded.

Ten rows marked complete across three tracking documents have a test-case reference column naming no actual test: four point at a requirement rather than a test, and six are left with a dash. That column links a business rule to the tests verifying it, so these rows trace to nothing, and checks built on the column have nothing to disagree with. Each row's reference should be corrected to point at its actual covering test.

One spec's execution-ledger table still uses an older, narrower set of columns, while the shared template now declares more columns and row groupings, and only one workflow phase may change a ledger's shape. Until that migration runs, a row needing a newer column has nowhere to record it, and at least one blank cell is silently read downstream as a default rather than flagged as missing.

A recorded test observation still refers to an old revision of the codebase, but the test it describes has since changed twice to align with newer rules. The check that flags this is correctly reporting it as stale now that it has enough history to detect it; the recorded observation should be refreshed to match the current test.

Report that a specification document and a generated onboarding instructions file still describe the project's README handling and an older compatibility window as they were before a deliberate change, because the documentation was never updated afterward. Ask for both to be corrected to match current behavior.

The file-finding module doesn't support filtering results by file owner or group. Please add user and group parameters so it can locate files owned by a specific user and/or group within a directory tree.

The guardrails command only prints human-formatted markdown text and has no branch in the argument parser for a machine-readable output format, so asking it for JSON output fails as a usage error instead of returning structured data. Since this command doubles as a pass/fail gate, that leaves the only signal it produces unparseable by anything automated. Please add JSON output support alongside the existing text format.

An interactive language tour's language-selection page doesn't list several actively maintained community translations, even though current, production-quality versions exist for a handful of additional languages hosted in a dedicated translation repository. Please add links to those maintained translations on the selection page.

Currently the tool refuses to let a resource mix ephemeral values with values that must persist in its stored state, but several real resource types naturally produce both kinds together, such as a private key that should never be stored alongside a public key or metadata that should. Proposes opt-in support so a resource can keep some attributes ephemeral while still persisting the rest.

fs.readFile and fs.readFileSync allocate a new buffer on every call, which is costly on hot paths; concurrent reads from multiple worker threads contend heavily on a kernel memory lock, measured at about seventeen times longer waits than doing the same work with separate child processes. Add an option to pass in a caller-supplied buffer to fill, keeping the convenience of the higher-level function.

Propose adding a pre-tool-use hook to a coding assistant's configuration that blocks the hook-bypass flag on commit and push commands, since that flag currently lets pre-commit checks, commit-message validation, and pre-push tests be silently skipped. The proposed fix is to add an existing published hook package to the configuration.

A particular Linux distribution built on openEuler isn't recognized as part of the RedHat OS family in the collected system facts, even though the openEuler base distribution itself already is. Please add it to that family mapping so the fact resolves consistently, matching what people currently have to work around downstream.

Please add a new telemetry client identifier value for a code editor's client-info string, so telemetry from that editor's language-server client is recognized correctly instead of falling into an unrecognized bucket. The expected outcome is that this client shows up as its own named value in the telemetry configuration going forward.

Command-line client binaries distributed for macOS through common channels are currently unsigned. In enterprise environments with strict binary-authorization policies, anything lacking a code signature is refused execution automatically. Could the macOS client release binaries be signed as part of the release process, to reduce risk and satisfy those policies?

When watch mode restarts the process after a file change, it gives no indication of which file actually triggered the restart, making it harder to understand why a restart just happened. Requests that watch mode print the name of the changed file alongside its restart message.

With the combined workspace-and-harness picker turned on, the hover text on those picker controls should show the user's actual configured keybinding instead of a fixed one, so the shortcut is discoverable without opening keyboard settings. It isn't decided yet what the hover should show when no keybinding is configured.

Request that two picker context menus in an editor's agents window offer a Configure Keybinding option, matching other configurable workbench controls, so right-clicking either picker opens the keyboard-shortcuts view focused on the matching command. The exact visual placement of the new menu entries is still open.

A rotating welcome phrase shown above the new-session input isn't announced to screen readers when a new session starts. Please announce it once when the composer appears and a screen reader is active, add a setting enabled by default to turn the announcement off, and mention how to disable it both in the announcement and in the accessibility docs. The exact wording and timing of the announcement are still open.

The new-session composer feels static and impersonal. Add an optional, default-off experimental setting that rotates a small set of short greeting phrases each time a new composer opens, personalized with the user's first name from their signed-in profile when available, falling back to a generic phrase otherwise. The exact tone and rotation of phrases is still open to feedback once it's built and can be tuned.

An enterprise policy can block AI features on client versions below a required minimum. When blocked, chat should show an update notice, the main editor should show a banner explaining why AI is unavailable while other editor features stay usable, and a separate agent window should show a blocking overlay instead of a banner. The exact visual treatment for each surface is still undecided.

In the experimental composer layout for the agent session window, controls describing workspace context are arranged differently between a new session and an already-running one, so equivalent controls don't line up. Expected: under the new layout and picker settings, the new-session composer should order its pickers consistently, right-aligned, with visual order matching keyboard order; exact spacing is still open for a design pass.

The MCP server UI shows disabled-looking controls without explaining what they mean, so when a server is off globally but on for one workspace, it's hard to tell if it's active and why. Reproduce by disabling a server globally, enabling it for one workspace, then checking its state in the UI; it should clearly show the effective state and its source, though the exact visual treatment isn't settled.

Request that a list of configured MCP servers stop showing each server's full path inline, since long or sensitive paths make the view noisy; expect the path to remain visible only in a details view while entries stay grouped by source location. The exact visual treatment of the list is still open.

In the chat tab menu, the Copy Link action currently sits somewhere in the middle of the list; please relocate it so it becomes the last item in that list instead. The exact position relative to the other bottom items is still open to discussion.

The rule limiting what runs on a documentation-only pull request is written as an exact set of four job names, and that measure is now outdated — it currently blocks a change that would speed up the pipeline without adding any of the cost the rule exists to prevent. Express the limit as a cost bound instead of a fixed job-name list. This changes an existing check's meaning, so anything relying on the current exact-match behavior needs updating.

An internal server method carries an old undocumented alias kept only for backward compatibility, possibly used as an unofficial extension point. Nothing in the core codebase calls it directly except one caller preserving that hook. Proposal: deprecate the alias, then remove it later and have that caller use the renamed method directly. Since external code may depend on it, this needs a maintainer's sign-off first.

Several C API functions and global configuration variables used for interpreter initialization have been deprecated since an earlier feature release and were scheduled for removal in an upcoming one. Proposes actually removing them now, which will break any embedder still calling the old initialization APIs directly, and requires updating the tests, the documented contract, and the docs alongside the code change.

Three acceptance-criteria entries in one spec are each declared twice, which the validator flags as duplicate-ID errors. An already-approved change plan covers renumbering the duplicates, including a fallback for when the originally planned number has since been taken by another change; please apply that already-approved plan.

Following a parent item that already settled the design, add three reminder hooks that surface a design-interview rule to the coding agent at moments it is often skipped: before a design document is written, before work is delegated, and before a plan is finalized. Each hook only reminds and never blocks, addressing how easy the rule is to forget there.

An earlier change did a purely mechanical rename of an authorization interface as a first step, with a follow-up change planned to reintroduce a helper function that uses the new interface's added capabilities, kept as its own clean diff. Please add that helper function now, following the plan already agreed in the earlier change.

A documented rule already governs how an agent phrases pull requests, issues, and markdown: cut the obvious, skip the play-by-play, stay plain. No such rule covers what appears on a screen, so the same problems show up visually - a needless intro paragraph, hint text under every field, a tooltip repeating a button's own label. This is one piece of an already-settled cleanup; write and apply the on-screen version of that rule.

The scheduler package depends on a shared controller package only for one small helper function used in a single test file. Since the function is simple, the dependency could be dropped by copying it into the scheduler's own code instead. This depends on a related, already-approved change landing first; once it merges, any allow-list entry it introduced should also be removed in the same change.

Part of a larger, already-approved plan, and depends on an earlier task in that plan defining the marker format a deliberate shortcut should carry. The rule asks an author taking a shortcut to mark it with an upper bound and the trigger that removes it, but nothing collects those markers, so one can go stale silently while still looking tracked. Expected: add a lane that walks the codebase, collects every marker, and reports them grouped by file.

A prior change added the ability to transfer TCP server and socket handles between worker threads, but only on Unix. Add the Windows side too: handing a moved socket over to a different thread's event loop needs to be connected to that loop's I/O completion port, following the same design already agreed for the Unix side.

Following an already-approved decision, add a deterministic writer, or an equivalent automated harness, that produces a build-system configuration file from a finalized design document, since no such writer exists yet and an agent currently performs the step by hand. Expect the related automated test to pass once the writer exists.

Loading multiple plugins in the current release corrupts standard-library type information, causing real programs to panic at runtime; this worked correctly in the previous release line. A backport of the fix to the next patch release has already been requested and approved by the person responsible for backport decisions, so it just needs to be applied.

An already-approved design change needs to be applied to the code, not just the contracts: right now, three of the CLI's automated routes never reach their first spec-bound stage because only one kind of result actually binds a spec. Wire the other decision paths to bind a spec too, so those three currently-blocked workflows can complete, and update the failing end-to-end coverage that's tracked against this gap.

A native extension behind an XML tree API still accepts byte-string input in four places, left from an old translation, even though the Python implementation only accepts text and a settled decision declared bytes unsupported. Because of this, some lookup functions silently return empty results for byte input instead of raising the expected error. Remove the remaining bytes support to match the settled decision.

A helper function in the email header-parsing module catches every exception with a bare except clause, silently swallowing errors it shouldn't. Proposes narrowing it to catch only the specific header-parsing error type, matching how the rest of the callers within that same module already handle it.

About twenty source comments across five files describing a design-trace check are written as a history of what earlier code changes did, rather than stating the rule that applies now. Rewrite them to state only the current behavior and the reason for it, following the project's own writing standard.

Report that two identifiers in a cross-project source file are misspelled, causing a panic-buffer variable name to read incorrectly. Propose the concrete fix of renaming both identifiers to their correctly spelled forms.

A fixtures directory contains three files that nothing in the codebase reads anymore; a full-tree search only turns up two unrelated historical references to the old location. They were originally documentation examples that ended up in the wrong place, and the real files they were meant to represent now live somewhere else. Please remove the unused directory.

A legacy test module was originally written to give a minimal smoke test to every standard-library module that wasn't tested elsewhere, but over time its list has shrunk to a single remaining entry, and that one module is already covered by another test file along with the other modules it happens to import. Since the file no longer serves its original purpose, it looks safe to delete outright.

A reference document about scaling review ceremony opens with the same explanatory paragraph twice, in slightly different wording, with the second copy's cross-reference pointing elsewhere. The file's history shows this came from a merge combining two versions instead of keeping one. Remove the duplicate paragraph and keep one consistent version with a correct cross-reference.

A scheduling feature added for the current release was implemented as a quick, tightly coupled addition directly inside the core scheduler's internal function, as a deliberate shortcut to ship on time. For the next release, proposes decoupling that logic out of the scheduler struct so the workload-aware preemption behavior instead runs as a normal collection of registered plugins reporting results the way other preemption logic already does.

A function that resolves ties between two scoring options by weight has no caller anywhere in the codebase, is exercised only by its own test, and isn't exposed on the package's public surface either. An existing test already documents why it can't safely be wired up: it references a weight value that nothing in the current data or intake actually produces.

Report that a conditional branch in an argument-validation helper still reassigns an exit code to the value it already defaults to, making the branch dead code that misleadingly implies one command type is still special-cased for exit codes, the same wrong belief that once caused a different command to return an incorrect exit code. Ask for the dead branch to be removed.

The comment documenting Math.sign in the standard library type definitions has an awkward grammatical phrasing, inconsistent with how nearby similar functions describe their parameter. Please fix the wording to match the other entries in the same file.

The README documents flags for several CLI commands but lists none for the init command, not even the flag the tool's own fix message points operators to run. A different init flag shows up only once, buried in unrelated prose elsewhere in the doc, not in the command's actual flag list. Please document the init command's flags properly in the README.

A contributor guide's section on a development overlay links to a more detailed reference document. Following that link produces a page-not-found error, and reloading the broken page shows the same result. Please fix the link so it points to a document that actually exists.

Generator-based coroutines were removed from the async I/O library as of an earlier feature release, but the documentation never says so. Proposes adding a note about the removal to the awaitables section, mentioning the resulting error when creating a task from one, and adding a version-changed note to the coroutine-checking function.

Several comments across a handful of the larger command and configuration source files still narrate what a prior version of the code used to do, instead of stating the rule that holds today. A related cleanup already rewrote this style of comment in one area; the same rewrite should be done for the remaining files as a separate sweep.

Report that the documentation for two array search methods describes returning the index of a matching value but omits stating that they return negative one when nothing matches, since that clause was left out of the written description. Ask for the missing clause to be added back.

A skill's documentation is missing a line break between two list items, so the second bullet renders as plain text appended to the sentence above it instead of as its own list item. That swallowed bullet happens to state the primary completion condition for the whole skill, so the formatting slip hides an important requirement. Please add the missing line break.

The example in the crypto-capability-checking documentation page uses an initialization vector length that isn't valid for the AES mode it demonstrates. Running the example as written on a fresh copy of the current runtime hits the invalid-length error at that step. Please fix the example's IV length so it runs cleanly.

A reference document describing a UI-definition protocol is written in a language other than the project's standard documentation language, even though the language rule covers every tracked document. Existing non-English content elsewhere is a backlog, but this file ships directly to downstream users, so it should be translated ahead of the rest. Please translate it to the standard language.

On a Korean-language legacy documentation page about adding the library to a website, clicking the link labeled as the JSX example HTML file leads to a missing-page error rather than the file it should open. Steps to see it: open that documentation page and click the linked example file; it should instead load the referenced HTML example.

Calling find, some, or every on a readable stream doesn't destroy the stream once a match is found, unless the source has already ended: with the stream still open and no further chunk arriving right after the match, it should still close as soon as the match is found. This reproduces reliably on any long-lived stream, such as one following a running process's output, and happens on any platform.

Report that under an experimental bundler chunking flag, a page renders its initial server HTML successfully and then never becomes interactive, with no error shown anywhere, because a chunk the client needs at runtime is never injected so the client-side registration call waits indefinitely. Reproduce by building and serving the page with the flag on versus off; expect the page to hydrate normally.

A command-line flag meant only for the setup command is silently accepted and ignored by every other command, so a typo in the target path passes validation and the command runs against whatever directory the process happens to be in. One of those commands writes a report file, so a mistyped path can overwrite output in the wrong project rather than failing with an error. The flag should be rejected outside setup, or honored there.

A check that decides whether a waiver's cited rule exists looks it up only among this run's own findings plus a short static list, so a real rule that simply didn't fire this run is reported unknown and its waiver silently dropped. Fixing a separate bug that keeps that rule from ever firing would flip this check on and reject an otherwise-valid waiver. The lookup needs a full list of real rules, not just the ones seen now.

On iOS 26.1 Safari specifically, combining a view-transition element that enters with another that exits at the same time causes a hard crash where the browser tab itself dies, not just a script error. A minimal online sandbox reproduces the crash reliably. Please investigate the interaction between simultaneous enter and exit view transitions that triggers this on that browser and OS version.

When a cross-crate extern item implementation has a default body marked to always inline, the compiler can inline that default directly into a caller in the same crate, even after another crate later provides an explicit override. The caller then silently keeps running the default behavior instead of the explicit implementation. A minimal test file reproducing the exact sequence is available.

The synchronous zstd compression function doesn't validate the size that was pledged for the input, so a call that should throw an error instead silently succeeds with the wrong result. To reproduce: call the compression function with a pledged size that doesn't match the actual input length and see that no error is raised.

Report that a checkpoint verification step passes an entire comma-separated list of test selectors into a single test-name filter, so when a selector list is used, the test runner matches nothing, silently runs zero tests, and still exits successfully. Reproduce by giving the checkpoint a selector cell with more than one entry and observing success with nothing actually run.

During project setup, two shipped review-instruction files are always skipped whenever they already exist in the target project, with no way to force an overwrite, unlike a very similar sibling file that does respect an overwrite flag. That means a fix to either of those two files never reaches a project that was already set up. Please make them respect the overwrite option the same way the sibling file does.

Running the kuberc set command with an empty option or flag name is accepted without any error, and it writes an entry with a blank name into the kuberc config file. Later, when a matching command tries to apply that entry, it fails with an invalid-flag error instead. The set command should reject an empty flag name up front instead of persisting a config that breaks things later.

A large automated build sweep across the community package ecosystem, run on a beta compiler release, surfaced a panic when formatting a bitflags-style value that didn't panic on the prior stable release. A log from the sweep and a partial minimized reproduction show the crash. Investigate what changed between the last known-good stable release and the beta causing this panic.

A compiler-internal panic now happens on the nightly channel that does not happen on the current stable release, reported as unreachable code hit inside a layout-computation function after normalizing a rigid type alias. The report includes an automatically minimized reproduction that reliably triggers the panic on the affected nightly builds; it did not reproduce on the last known-good stable version.

Using a loop construct together with a delegated-host setting that references the loop item no longer works, raising an 'item is undefined' error, even though this combination used to work in an older release. This is a recurrence of a very similar problem that was reported and seemingly fixed once before.

Report that the integration for the self-hosted uptime-monitoring tool Uptime Kuma fails authentication against a newer major version of that monitor, even with a freshly generated, valid API key, because the integration sends the key as the basic-auth username instead of the password the newer server expects. It worked correctly before the upgrade; expect successful authentication after a fix.

After upgrading to the newest monthly release, a solar charge controller integration's 'yield yesterday' sensor lost its statistics state class, and the system now logs a warning that it can't generate long-term statistics for that entity. It worked fine on the previous monthly release. To reproduce, upgrade an installation using that integration and check the sensor afterward; it should keep its state class like before.

A recent change that enabled a new cross-crate-info merging mode broke the documentation search box — searching by full path, partial path, or just the type name all fail to surface a struct that's clearly documented on its own page. This worked before that change landed and has been bisected to it, only failing on the nightly channel since. Please fix the regression or revert the change that caused it.

Inside the project's own test-runner environment, checking installed metadata for the core package fails to find it, and listing installed packages omits it too, on the two most recent release lines; the same check worked on the prior line. A minimal reproduction using a CI action is available, and a proposed fix already exists. Please review and land the fix.

In a version released after 24.15, marking a readable stream destroyed before pushing a null end-of-stream signal now drops the final chunk when the stream runs through a raw-deflate decompression transform, which didn't happen on 24.15. A short reproduction script is available: it builds a pseudo-random buffer, compresses it, and feeds it through a custom readable stream that hits this exact destroy-then-push-null sequence.

Auto-import suggestions skip a folder's index or barrel file when the imported folder's name happens to be a prefix of the name of the file doing the importing, pointing straight at the inner module file instead. This changed between two specific editor releases and used to correctly suggest the barrel path before; a small example project shows the folder layout that triggers it.

Report that with an experimental test-proxy feature enabled, a request opening a raw TCP socket and waiting for an echoed byte never resolves, no response, error, or timeout, in a recent release, whereas the same request worked in the immediately preceding release. Reproduce with a minimal route opening a plain socket with the flag on, compared against the flag off.

A helper function that lists the child process IDs of a given process walks the entire system process list four separate times to do it, which is unnecessarily expensive. It should be possible to collect the same information in a single pass instead.

The lint job in CI hits its ten-minute limit even though every individual step inside it reports success, so the whole job gets marked cancelled and blocks merging with no actual test failure to point to. One real run measured just over ten minutes end to end. Parallelize the workflow down to the smallest independent unit — the open question is how fine to split it, and whether that needs new job boundaries or just reordering.

An internal virtual-file-system layer for project-reference type declarations allocates an excessive number of strings, reproduced by generating type-check configs for a large open-source app and opening one of its core files with a custom type-check config name set. Please investigate and reduce the unnecessary string allocation in that layer.

Looking at the most recent successful run on the main branch, the lint CI job took about two minutes against a ten-minute budget. Measurement shows eighteen independent commands making up most of that job run one after another, alongside a separate slower lane bounding part of the job on its own. Proposes starting the independent commands together and splitting the file behind the slower lane's time, to cut the job's wall time.

Calling hasattr on an attribute backed by an empty slot is measured at about 241 nanoseconds, versus roughly 33.5 nanoseconds when there's no slot at all for that name, a large gap for what should be a fast check. A fix has already been proposed separately; compare the two timeit benchmarks to see the difference yourself.

Report that two process-spawning test files sit in the same test project and so share one continuous-integration job and its CPU cores with every other file there, causing contention that slows the whole job. Measured timing shows running the two files concurrently did not speed up the second file and slowed the first, compared to running them one at a time.

When the kubelet runs at a common debug verbosity, it logs a 'label not found' warning for every optional container annotation that's simply absent. On a cluster with around 220 pods and two containers each, this floods the log fast enough to fill up disk space quickly. To reproduce, run kubelet at that verbosity with many pods lacking those annotations; move logging to a quieter level or stop assuming the annotation must be present.

A validator that expands a citation graph beyond the tree it already crawled re-walks the entire expanded graph from scratch on every pass, both when rebuilding the reachable-document set and when rescanning for citations that still don't resolve. Each pass only discovers a little new information, so the repeated full re-walk gets slower as the tree grows. It should only revisit what changed since the last pass, not the whole graph every time.

In a long chat session with the AI agent feature, the component that tracks file-change diffs hooks every earlier turn's diff computation to the live chat stream again. So every token streamed for the current turn makes it re-parse all earlier responses, and CPU stays high for the whole session. Please stop recomputing turns that are already finished.

A regex the citation scanner uses to find documents a skill references is quadratic over a long unbroken run of path-like characters with no recognized file extension, because the scanner tries a match at each position in that run and backtracks through what follows. Timing it against a single repeated character shows scan time growing sharply as the run lengthens, risking a serious bottleneck on adversarial input.

When middleware adds a Set-Cookie header carrying an auth token to a static, prerendered page, the framework doesn't exclude that response from the page's year-long cache header, so a CDN can cache and serve one user's auth token to other users. Reproduce by building and requesting the linked example page and observing both headers together. This needs sign-off before a fix ships, given the security impact.

Report a static, medium-severity security concern: generated reviewer instructions conditionally load a review-policy document without pinning it to a trusted revision, so a contributor could add or modify that document in an untrusted change, and a tool-enabled reviewer might then treat the contributor's own instructions as review policy. The cause is the missing trusted-revision pin.

A function that turns a user-configured exclusion pattern into a regular expression passes it straight into the regex constructor without sanitizing it, so a crafted pattern can trigger catastrophic backtracking and hang the process during auto-import resolution. A different, similarly named preference already escapes its pattern safely. The vulnerable one needs the same kind of escaping or validation applied.

In the SSH channel handling, an attacker can trigger a full connection deadlock by sending a crafted sequence of messages once a channel exists, denying service to other users. Fix it by handling every defined channel message type explicitly, treating anything unexpected as a protocol error, and closing the connection right away instead of buffering. Already investigated and approved through a private security process; ship it as approved.

In an experimental package implementing a transport protocol, the padding added to an initial handshake packet isn't counted against the anti-amplification limit restricting how much data a server may send before a client's address is confirmed. This can let a server send more data than the limit permits under some circumstances, and was reported as a potential security issue. Please fix the accounting so padding counts correctly.

When the node agent is configured with a manifest URL and header values carrying credentials such as bearer tokens or API keys, those values get written into its startup logs in plain text. The code building the static-pod source config copies the header map straight into a log call without masking it, even though that field is already treated as secret and redacted elsewhere in the same codebase, including a separate config-dump path.

When a Server Component passes a nested object holding a server-only environment variable to a Client Component, the framework's serializer includes every key of that object in the client bundle, even ones the client never uses, exposing values meant to stay server-side. To reproduce: build or run the app, pass such an object across the server-to-client boundary, then inspect the page's HTML or client bundle for the sensitive values.

Report that an editor's connector-protocol HTTP transport follows redirects while checking only the destination's protocol scheme and removing just four commonly named credential headers, so an allow-or-deny policy is never re-evaluated against where the redirect lands, letting a blocked server receive a session via a permitted redirector, and letting other credential headers leak to the new host; expect that check to run there too.

In the SSH multiplexing code, a channel that's registered but not yet fully established could have its incoming-request queue flooded by a malicious peer, deadlocking the whole connection. The fix adds an atomic flag marking when a channel becomes usable, and until then drops every packet except the open confirmation or failure, without blocking or tearing down the connection.

The iSCSI volume plugin builds its metadata file path by joining an API-supplied identifier into the path, and because path joining normalizes '..' segments, a crafted identifier can make it write outside its own plugin directory. The identifier's validation regex is too permissive and lets almost anything through, so a malicious value passes admission. Tighten the regex to reject path-traversal segments and harden the path construction too.

Calling the runtime's DNS-server-configuration function with an address specifying port zero crashes the process with a native abort, reproducing reliably every time on a specific recent release. The call should complete without throwing or crashing. A native stack trace pointing into the DNS resolution library is attached. Please fix the crash so port zero is handled without aborting.

The compiler crashes with an internal panic reporting that unreachable code was hit inside opaque-type handling in the type-checking pass, triggered by a small standalone source file. A full internal error trace and the exact triggering source were captured at the time of filing.
Running a plan against a particular AWS resource and import configuration crashes Terraform with a full Go panic and stack trace instead of producing a plan.

Report that the infrastructure tool crashes after upgrading a Helm-related provider to its next major version. A crash log with a stack trace is attached, and it reproduces by applying a configuration that manages a Helm release together with a module computing a configuration-directory hash as one of its input values.

Running plan against a specific resource type crashes with a nil pointer dereference panic on a recent alpha build. An older commit, built locally, does not have this problem. Debug output and a crash trace were captured and are attached; plan should complete without panicking.

Compiling a small snippet where a function takes a generic wrapper type whose trait bound isn't satisfied crashes the compiler with an internal error, 'unexpected sort of node', instead of just reporting the ordinary unsatisfied-trait-bound error it produces first. I have the minimal reproduction code and the full panic output with the internal error name and location.

Assigning a type through a chain of trait blanket implementations crashes the compiler with a segmentation fault, and a backtrace is attached. The underlying cause is a stack overflow, triggered by a deliberately contrived use of blanket implementations rather than realistic code. Please guard against the overflow so this produces a normal compiler error instead of a crash.

Running the built-in test command against a test configuration that includes a failed assertion crashes the tool while it tries to display the run's result, instead of printing the failure normally. Debug output from the crash, including the tool's own version and the versions of its internal dependencies at the time, is available alongside the test configuration files that trigger it.

After applying a configuration and opening the interactive console, typing a reference to a resource's attribute causes a panic naming a 'value is marked' internal error, along with a stack trace, instead of showing the resource's attributes or a normal error message.

Report that a recent patch release of the infrastructure tool crashes while showing a previously saved plan file in machine-readable format, inside a continuous-integration job. A crash log with a stack trace is attached, and it reproduces by running the show command with the JSON output flag against a downloaded plan file.

After a small fix meant to recover diagnostics that were previously getting lost, a race condition in the ephemeral resources test suite became visible, which it wasn't reliably showing before. To reproduce, apply that separate fix, edit a specific line in the ephemeral resources code, and run the test suite with the race detector enabled a few times; it fails intermittently rather than on every run.

Calling unref on a socket occasionally throws a TypeError trying to read an internal timeout symbol off of undefined, but only sporadically — in a system handling significant traffic we see just a few occurrences a day, not on every call. I have a minimal artificial reproduction plus a more realistic one where something upstream sets the socket handle to undefined before unref runs.

When a native addon invokes a JS callback with a pending exception, and that callback's error-logging call itself throws, uncaught-exception handling and the inspector console hook call each other in an infinite loop, locking up the process instead of reporting the error. This is hard to reproduce deterministically since it depends on timing. Please break the recursive loop between the two handlers.

When a build uses both a CSS preprocessor config file and at least one Sass-based stylesheet, two internal worker pools race to write the same shared runtime file. On a cold build in a large enough app, modules going through the preprocessor fail intermittently, with which ones fail and how many varying run to run. A minimal reproduction project with a handful of source files, built from a cleared cache, reliably shows the race.

Applying a configuration that uses filesystem functions whose result ends up carrying two internal value markers intermittently fails Terraform's own internal consistency check, even though the exact same configuration sometimes applies successfully. Debug output from both a passing and a failing apply is available to compare.

Report a race condition where a networking library automatically drains an HTTP response body in the background, so if a caller closes the response early and then reads trailer headers anyway, those trailers can be populated unpredictably by the background drain, making the outcome intermittent. A fix for the underlying draining logic is already being worked on.

A specific runtime build occasionally hangs for hours during process shutdown when embedded in another project's build pipeline, rather than shutting down normally. It isn't reliably reproducible, but was observed roughly three to five times across about two months of near-daily builds, so maybe one in thirty runs. Shutdown should complete without hanging.

On a particular JavaScript runtime option when deployed to a hosting platform, requests to routes that should be served via a rewrite intermittently return the root page with a 200 status instead of the expected rewritten route. It doesn't happen on every request — a repeated-request script against the same deployment shows it failing only some of the time. I have a minimal reproduction app and a script that shows the failure.

Running with a high number of parallel worker processes, a number of SSH connections intermittently fail, throwing a generic session-not-active error; re-running the playbook usually succeeds for those hosts while a different unpredictable set may fail instead. This is intermittent and tied to parallelism level. A reproduction and a proposed fix are available. Please land the fix.

A CLI tool that spawns the compiler's API in a subprocess and checks its output occasionally sees an unexpected 'context canceled' message on the error stream in automated CI test runs, instead of the expected empty output. It happens sporadically, consistently on one CI OS, sometimes on another, never on a third, with different test cases failing each time. A standalone reproduction project spawning the same subprocess repeatedly is available.

The recently added state-file locking only treats an 'already exists' error as meaning someone else holds the lock, and rethrows anything else. On Windows, though, creating a file exclusively fails with a permission error rather than an already-exists error, so every state write fails hard there, and the specific test case the locking feature was built to pass cannot pass on that platform.

Report that after upgrading a home-automation platform from one recent monthly release to the next, a voice-assistant integration stops reporting any devices online, even though the same devices are confirmed reachable through the vendor's own mobile app. It worked correctly on the prior release; expect devices to report online again after the upgrade.

The Shelly Camera integration can discover and configure a specific camera model correctly, including its motion sensor, but once password protection is enabled directly on the camera, the video stream fails with a server error, even though the integration can still authenticate using that same password. It works fine when no password has been set on the device.

Fact gathering fails when running against QNX Neutrino 6.5.0 under Python 3.9, because the routine checking whether a network-lookup patch is needed queries a port as a bare number, omitting the socket type and protocol - a combination that OS documents as invalid. Since the check itself fails, the patch it exists to test can't be evaluated. Fix it by passing an explicit socket family and type there, keeping its fallback.

Building a build-infrastructure tool for a specific operating system fails to compile, traced to a known compatibility bug in an upstream gRPC client library on that OS. The fix already landed in a newer upstream release. Please bump the pinned dependency version to the fixed release so the build compiles again.

A CSS file that begins with a byte-order-mark character, which is valid under the CSS specification, causes both the dev server and the production build to fail outright instead of being handled. Steps to reproduce: include such a file in the app and run a build. Expected behavior is that the build succeeds and treats the marker the way the specification requires, rather than raising an error.

The scanner that finds managed rule sections inside fenced code blocks treats a list-marker line as closing the fence even when a different fence character opened it, so content like a dash before tildes inside a tilde fence is wrongly read as the closing delimiter, and the real closing fence is then read as a new opener.
