This makes a managed section stop being recognized; it should follow CommonMark's own fence-delimiter rules.

Report that a URL-pattern matching API creates the properties of its result object in an order that does not match the order the web standard's interface description specifies, observable through property enumeration even though direct access is unaffected. Reproduce by matching a pattern and enumerating the result's own keys; expect the order to match what browsers and the standard produce.

A tool deciding whether an HTML comment hides following content is stricter than GitHub's markdown renderer: GitHub hides content under both the uppercase comment marker and a lowercase lookalike, but the local check only recognizes the uppercase form. To reproduce, send a lowercase-variant body to GitHub's rendering API and compare it to the local checker's answer; they disagree. The checker should match GitHub's rendering for both cases.

For an HTTP CONNECT request made without an explicit Host header, the generated Host header reflects where the TCP socket actually connects — the proxy itself — rather than the request-target, which should be the tunnel's real destination. This happens on every CONNECT call, not just occasionally. The applicable HTTP specification says the Host header should reflect the request-target, so this needs fixing to conform.

A layered ignore-pattern matcher disagrees with the underlying version-control tool when a later rule re-includes a directory an earlier rule excluded: the tool re-includes just the entry, while the matcher re-includes everything beneath it. This was measured against the exact pattern block the initializer writes, and the two disagree. Since this is silently wrong with no error, fix the directory-negation handling.

On a 64-bit ARM Linux target, aggregates of a few matching integer fields are passed and returned with machine code that doesn't match equivalent C code under the same calling convention, while the same case with floating-point fields behaves correctly. A small sample comparing the two languages' generated code is available; the cause appears to be mishandling of a homogeneous-aggregate calling-convention rule for that architecture.

When a stream iterator's broadcast or share cancellation is given a falsy reason value, calling next afterward returns a clean end-of-stream instead of rejecting or throwing with that reason. The async form should reject and the sync form should throw with the exact reason supplied, regardless of whether that reason happens to be falsy.

Report that a stream-sharing iterator helper configured to drop the newest item eagerly pulls more data from its upstream source than it should, instead of waiting until buffer space is available. Reproduce by taking two items from a fast consumer in quick succession; the second call should discard only one buffered result and then wait, but instead drains the upstream immediately.

On the s390x architecture, the code that handles return values from native library calls doesn't widen integer types smaller than the machine word size, even though the underlying native-call library's documented contract requires that widening. This causes a real failure when a certain code-analysis library is loaded through that mechanism on that architecture. The calling code should widen narrow return types as the contract requires.

A WASI pthread test in the test suite fails intermittently with a WASM runtime error, 'unreachable', surfaced through an assertion failure in the underlying C code before the runtime trap. I have the failing run's stderr output and stack trace showing exactly where it happens. This test needs to be quarantined as flaky and investigated separately from other failures.

A test covering a locking mechanism for file provenance failed once in a pipeline on a change that didn't touch that code area, then passed on a local re-run of the same commit and a later pipeline re-run with no changes. Two earlier reports already recorded this same file as intermittently failing on load, so this looks like a recurrence with a different symptom than either. Please re-investigate the root cause.

DISABLED test_flash_attention_vs_math_ref_grads_batch_size_8_seq_len_q_2048_seq_len_k_2048_head_dim_8_is_causal_False_dropout_p_0_48_bfloat16_scale_l1_enable_gqa_True_n_heads0_sdpa_backend_ck_cuda_bfloat16 — filed automatically by a flaky-test bot after intermittent CI failures on one accelerator backend: 3 of 6 recent workflow runs flaky, 4 failures against 3 successes.

A test verifying that a stale lock can be taken over without removing an active one fails intermittently in CI under load, even on documentation-only changes unrelated to locking. Timing shows the test's cases sit right at their pass or fail limits even when they succeed, with one case observed taking over twenty seconds locally under load against a much shorter expected wait.

Report, filed automatically by a bot, that the test DISABLED test_redispatch_nn_functional_linear_cross_entropy_chunked_cuda_float16 was disabled after being confirmed genuinely flaky, measured at fourteen failures against ten successes across recent runs. Ask that it be investigated rather than assumed fine because the pipeline currently shows green.

A set of tests that spawn a full project setup into a temporary sandbox fail intermittently under load, but pass every time when that file runs alone. Measured twice within minutes on an unchanged tree, roughly a third of those cases failed under load, while the file takes well under a minute alone. This looks like the same flakiness as an earlier, fixed case involving a different lock mechanism in the same family.

An autoscaling test that targets a custom resource is flaking across all four related CI jobs — the two periodic runs and the two presubmit runs that exercise this feature. I scanned every retained test-result file across roughly 400 builds over a recent three-month window and measured a distinct non-zero failure rate on each of the four jobs; the exact per-job numbers are in the scan output. This needs to be quarantined until it's fixed.

Two legs of the test matrix each spawn a shell process per test case, and both intermittently fail with the same runtime error about an invalid assembly name, even on changes touching no shell-related code. Every case in an affected run fails identically, and because the failure surfaces through whichever assertion reads the child's output, it misleadingly looks like that test itself is wrong. Please investigate the intermittent spawn failure.

A particular parallel test case is flaky and intermittently fails in continuous integration on the main branch; example failing CI run links were provided at filing time. Requests that it be skipped or otherwise quarantined until the underlying flakiness is diagnosed and fixed.

A lock-related test times out intermittently on high-load CI runners, observed across five different branches during a large sweep of open pull requests, none of which touched the locking code being tested. None of the affected changes have any causal path to the failing code and it doesn't reproduce locally even under load, which points to CI load rather than a real defect; re-running the same commit with no changes turns it green.

Report that a provider-initialization test can be affected by the local machine's own filesystem-based provider mirrors or CLI configuration files, making its outcome depend on the environment it runs in rather than being self-contained. Propose updating the test so it is isolated from such local machine state.

A test file still overrides the suite's default timeout down to a much shorter value left over from before the default was raised, even though its calls are expensive enough to need the longer one. An earlier attempt to find which files needed this fix miscounted by matching imports and comments as well as calls, wrongly flagging an extra file; the corrected count narrows it to four files. Remove the leftover short timeout override.

With a newer beta of the Tk toolkit, four ttk-related tests fail because they assert that an empty string is rejected for a couple of style options, but that empty string is now the documented default in the new Tk version and no longer raises an error. This isn't a bug in our code, just tests written against the old Tk behavior. Please update the tests to match the new Tk semantics.

A test for the initializer command fails only on one operating system and passes in the pipeline running a different one. The test builds its search text with a path-joining helper that uses platform-specific separators, but the actual output is always normalized to forward slashes. On the platform using backslashes, the expected text never occurs, so the search fails deterministically. Fix the test to search using the normalized format.

An integration test suite for user management on a BSD test target passes the first time it runs but fails on a second run against the same host, because an assertion checks that exactly one specific user exists without accounting for a leftover local user created by the previous run. Proposes having the test suite clean up the user it creates so repeated runs against the same host don't leave stale state behind.

A test that simulates a lock takeover starts a write without awaiting it, and nothing guarantees that write finishes before the test's revalidating read runs afterward. When the machine is quick enough, that write completes first and the test passes, but it failed on a slower CI job even on a documentation-only branch, showing the bug is in the test's timing assumptions rather than in what changed.

Report that a certificate-related conformance test fails every time on Linux nodes that still have the default, restricted unprivileged-port-range setting, because the test needs to bind a low-numbered privileged port that setting blocks. This is specific to that port-range configuration and does not reproduce on nodes using a different setting.

A test fixture uses a filename containing angle-bracket characters left over from an unfilled template placeholder, and those characters are illegal in Windows filenames. The test fails on Windows because the file it tries to create can never actually be written, so the assertion it's meant to check is never reached; it's unaffected on the Linux CI environment. Please fix the fixture name so it avoids reserved characters.

A test that's supposed to be gated on subinterpreter support imports an internal test-only extension module directly, and when that module isn't built or available, the test fails outright instead of skipping cleanly. The test needs a proper availability check or an import guard so its absence causes a clean skip, not a failure.

A validation helper checking whether a certain pipeline job step preserves failure signals has two rejection conditions with no covering test: one for an aggregating step with an extra step doing its own work, and one for an error-continuation flag set at the job level instead of the step level. Existing parameterized cases only exercise the step-level conditions. Add cases so removing either condition would cause a test to fail.

A particular end-to-end CI job has been failing since two specific pull requests merged on the same day, though the failure looks unrelated to what those changes touched and instead points to a container image being removed during the job. Reproducible by re-running the affected periodic job; it fails at a synchronized setup stage before any actual test runs.

A formatting-verification job started failing after a certain merge because the Go formatter produces different output on the arm64 architecture than on amd64, and the job has been consistently red on every run since all runs began landing on arm64 nodes. Right after that merge, results swung back and forth between passing and failing based on which architecture a given run happened to land on.

Report that kubelet version-skew continuous-integration jobs have failed consistently since a specific date, because the artifact host stopped serving release files for an old minor version that recently reached end of life, correctly catching that the jobs still depend on fetching that retired version's files. Before that date the same jobs passed reliably.

The commit-queue and auto-start continuous integration workflows have been failing since a specific date because a required package can't be found during install. This has stayed broken continuously since that point; please restore the missing dependency so the workflow can run again.

A test covering a specific feature-gated auth behavior has been failing consistently on the jobs that check compatibility between different kubelet and API server versions, and it's been red since a specific date I can pin down. This looks like a genuine regression the test correctly caught, not a flaky or badly written test. Please find what changed around that date and fix the regression rather than adjusting the test.

A continuous-integration job for the platform's node agent has failed since a specific date, traced to an upstream bug in a development runtime snapshot's HTTP client that cancels keep-alive requests reactivated after brief idle time. Under load this cascades into hundreds of unrelated log-retrieval test failures, though the platform's own code isn't at fault. Track the upstream fix and confirm the job passes once it lands.

A periodic end-to-end compatibility-versions job has not passed a single time since a release branch was cut, a complete failure rate, because the version validator never reads a minimum-compatibility value correctly, and the cut shifted which version pair the job validates. A comparison of the last passing run against the first failing one, with timestamps and the commit each used, is included as measurement.

Sandbox-permission integration tests for the agent host fail consistently on the macOS product build only; Windows, Linux, and the separate macOS pull-request check all still pass, and re-running doesn't help. The build was last green before a specific pair of changes that added those sandbox test cases, and has been red on every run since.

Report that a Windows code-coverage workflow has started failing on the main branch and a release-staging branch, likely because the hosted Windows runner image was updated to a newer version with different behavior, whereas the same step used to only produce a warning rather than a failure. The failure is specific to the updated Windows runner environment.

A CI job that runs unit tests against the bleeding-edge development build of the Go toolchain started failing, apparently after that upstream toolchain updated. The failure shows a specific test erroring while unmarshaling older checkpoint data into a newer structure, with a full error trace captured in the job log. This only affects the job built against the toolchain's development branch, not the pinned version.

The RHEL 10.0 test remote environment is broken: it's no longer possible to install the kernel modules package needed for the running kernel, which breaks the iptables test and other tests that depend on this specific OS remote. This is an environment or infrastructure problem with the RHEL 10.0 remote itself, not a code regression. Please get the remote's package availability fixed or pin a working kernel and package combination.

A shared pipeline setup action passes both a direct version input and a version-file input to a runtime-setup step together. When a caller intentionally requests the file-derived version, the direct input still ends up non-empty, so the step warns about both being set, even though the resulting version is correct. Only that lane emits the warning. Adjust the action so it doesn't pass both inputs together.

One of the project's continuous-build machines is currently reporting itself as dead and has been flagged as broken by the build dashboard. Requests that the infrastructure team look into and fix the offline build machine.

The release-tagging workflow succeeds when a release pull request merges, but its tag-push step is always skipped, so the tag is never created and the downstream publish workflow never starts. The check for whether the merge came from a release pull request reads a response field the API doesn't provide, so it always comes back false, and repeating the run gives the same result.

Report that a compiler bootstrap process builds automatic-differentiation and offload components before building the linker they depend on, so a clean build environment fails those later steps for lacking the linker on the path, and linking is also slow on such large object files. Propose moving the linker-related build steps earlier so the linker is ready in time.

An automated dependency-update tool can't push one of its update branches because a repository push-protection rule is rejecting it, so all of that tool's update pull requests are now paused as a precaution until it's resolved. Either the push rule needs an exception for that tool, or the tool needs to be granted a bypass so it can push its branches again.

In the lint configuration, one global variable declaration still uses the deprecated ESLint globals value instead of the current one, unlike the rest of the globals declared in that same block, which already use the current value. It's the only place left in the whole repository using the old value. Please update that one declaration to match the rest.

A type-checking gate meant to run the current stable compiler actually runs a forward-looking, not-yet-current one, because two installed packages both provide a command with the same binary name and the forward-looking one wins. Checking which binary a specific commit resolves to confirms this. So the stable gate isn't testing against the stable compiler, on every run. Resolve the naming collision.

The end-to-end test framework has several recurring problems bundled together: cleanup code across the suite discards errors from delete calls, hiding resource leaks; disruptive tests that restart control-plane components add to flakiness; and API-server timeouts cause hard-to-debug failures. A fix touching many files is proposed to address the error suppression, cleanup gaps, and related flakiness together.

Building on the ppc64le architecture gets blocked by an integration-test image that has reached end of life with no source available to build it for that architecture. Please exclude that image from the integration test run so builds aren't blocked by it.
Propose updating the toolchain used to build a WebAssembly target to a newer supported release, with the concrete fix already prepared as a linked change.

An open, auto-merging update would bump a markdown linter to a release needing a newer minimum Node.js version than this project declares as its floor. A contributor on the older declared Node version won't be able to run the markdown lint command locally, even though the hosted lint job would likely stay green since it runs the newest allowed Node. Stop that update auto-merging, or raise the declared floor.

A container vulnerability scan flags a known CVE in a tar-handling library, but that library doesn't appear anywhere in the project's own dependency tree or lockfile. Inspecting the built filesystem shows the framework itself bundles a vendored copy of that library internally. I'd expect the framework to ship a patched version of its vendored copy, or explain whether the flagged version is actually exploitable here.

A CSS-processing library bundled inside a web framework has a known arbitrary-file-read vulnerability in the currently bundled version, flagged by a dependency audit with several high-severity advisories on a freshly created project using the framework's latest stable release. A fixed version is already published upstream. Bump the bundled version to the fixed release or later.

A dependency scanning tool flagged that the compiled binary is built with a version of the language toolchain carrying a known TLS session-resumption vulnerability, where mutating certain fields on a cloned configuration between the initial and resumed handshake can let a resumed handshake wrongly succeed. Expected outcome: rebuild and ship using one of the already-patched toolchain versions that fixes the vulnerability.

Bump the bundled OpenSSL to its latest patch releases ahead of the next scheduled release; the highest severity among the fixed vulnerabilities is moderate and it isn't clear the project is directly affected, but it should be updated anyway as a precaution, along with CI and release artifacts. This is flagged as blocking the next release and needs release-manager sign-off.

Report that a vendored client library for a remote-state backend is on an old version that security scanners flag with several known vulnerabilities, and ask for it to be updated to a current, patched release. The maintainers have acknowledged the report, noting the dependency supports that remote-state backend.

A dependency pulled in to fix earlier security issues in a container-runtime library comes from a domain that goes down occasionally, and its own maintainer has said they plan to move it to more stable hosting eventually. Please track migrating to wherever that dependency ends up once the maintainer moves it, since the current source isn't reliable.

Please bump the vendored code-formatting tool dependency to its latest release. In that release, a previously controversial multi-line-call formatting rule became an opt-in extra rule that's disabled by default, and the remaining closing-parenthesis placement behavior was narrowed to a more specific case. Bumping it should reduce unwanted reformatting for users who don't opt into the extra rule.

The key-value store bundled with every currently supported release line of a container-orchestration platform carries dozens of known vulnerabilities, including a couple rated critical, and carries older dependencies than any other control-plane component. A scan confirms this across all supported lines, and a newer upstream release presumably fixing these is already available. Evaluate bumping the bundled version across supported lines.

The stable package repository's main component has served an empty package index for every supported Linux distribution, even though the signed repository metadata still validates correctly, so installing via the standard package manager fails everywhere it's configured. Expected behavior: installing should succeed. This needs release-management or infrastructure approval, since it's a broken published distribution channel, not a code bug.

The page hosting the project's published PGP public key now returns a bot-verification challenge instead of the key when fetched programmatically, breaking automated tools that resolve it. The key should be fetchable with a normal HTTP request the way it always was; fixing this needs release-manager approval since it touches the published key's own distribution.

Request that a contributor with a dozen already-merged changes be granted permission to trigger the project's automated trial builds on their own submissions without asking a reviewer each time. Whether to grant this is an open decision for the maintainers, who must approve it since granting build-trigger access is an operation only they can perform; once granted, the expectation is routine self-service access.

A package maintainer who owns the GitHub repository behind a published module wants its documentation hidden from the public package index, across all current and future versions, rather than retracting individual releases. This has to be actioned by whoever runs that hosted index, since it isn't something the maintainer or a contributor can trigger themselves. They understand this won't remove already-cached copies elsewhere.

Since a recent GPG key rotation on the package repository, installing the aarch64 RPM package fails signature verification, while the equivalent x86_64 package installs and verifies fine from the same repo. It looks like the aarch64 packages weren't re-signed with the rotated key, or the repo metadata wasn't updated. This needs a release manager to fix and confirm the aarch64 packages before closing.

A test for a new SIMD-related feature crashes with an illegal-instruction signal on a particular arm64 single-board-computer processor, and possibly similar chips. A maintainer requested the already-fixed underlying issue be considered for backport into the next upcoming minor release, since it's a broken new feature that should be corrected first. This needs release-team approval before it can be cherry-picked.

An automated source-rewrite tool, when moving a field assignment during a code-modernization rewrite, can produce a struct literal with the same field name listed twice, which fails to compile, because the rewrite doesn't check for an existing key before moving the assignment. A fix already approved for the current development branch needs to be backported into the next minor release, which needs release-manager approval.
Backport an already-approved fix for a consistently failing compiler test to the next minor release; the backport request has already been approved by the maintainers.

Request, following an approval already given elsewhere, that a fix for a crash triggered by a generic function combined with a pointer type parameter and an embedded interface be backported into the next minor release of the language toolchain, since it corrects a regression that could make a previously valid program panic at runtime. This backport needs a release manager's approval.

A code-fixing tool produces output with a comma inside a generated comment that then fails to compile. The fix for that has already been merged to the main branch and approved by the person who handles that release line's backport decisions; it just needs to be cherry-picked into the next patch release.

Please backport the already-merged fix for the mutex-profiling deadlock during Windows asynchronous preemption and GC into the upcoming minor release. The fix itself is settled and merged on the main branch already; this is just asking for it to be cherry-picked into the next patch release, which needs release-manager sign-off.

A change to a standard JSON-encoding function accidentally started invoking a custom text-marshaling method on map keys of string-based types, which it previously didn't, regressing behavior for callers relying on the old result. A maintainer requested this fix be considered for backport into the next upcoming minor release. This needs release-team approval before it can be cherry-picked.

A fix for the post-quantum key-encapsulation self-test, and a re-sealing of an earlier validated cryptographic module build, has already been approved on the main branch and needs to be backported into the next minor release's certified module build. Needs release-manager approval to pull that already-accepted change into the backport branch, since it affects a security-certified cryptographic module.

A change to relocation handling broke parsing of certain 32-bit PowerPC object files that parsed correctly before it, and also breaks regeneration of related system-call files for that platform. Backport the already-approved fix for this to the next minor release.

Request, citing an already-fixed defect in code-modernization tooling as the settled basis, that its fix be backported into the next minor release, because the defect causes an automated code-fix tool to produce code that fails to compile when a comment holds a comma inside a certain construct. This backport needs a release manager's approval.

This is a tracking placeholder for writing the release notes text covering an already-stabilized macro-related feature. The notes still need to be drafted: picking the right category, writing a short description of what changed, and deciding whether a compatibility note is needed.

This tracks writing the release-notes text for an already-merged compiler change that preserves an ambiguous glob lint for certain trait method picks. Someone needs to draft a short description of what changed, pick the right release-notes category, and note whether a compatibility notes section is needed. The underlying change itself is already settled; this is just the writeup.

This tracks writing the release-notes entry for a standard-library change stabilizing a new string-decoding function for a specific text encoding with explicit byte-order handling. The entry needs the right category and a concise description, and should consider whether a compatibility note or a prominent callout is warranted. Draft the release-notes text and get it approved before release.

Tracks drafting the release notes for an upcoming minor compiler release, compiled from the set of changes already merged for that version, including changes such as allowing a mutable reference's lifetime to be shortened during certain coercions. Needs contributors to review and edit the auto-generated draft entries for the changes they authored before the notes are finalized.

Draft the release-notes text for a change that stabilized a language type, following the standard release-notes process: specify the right category and a short description of what changed, and note whether a compatibility section is needed.

Track the release checklist for a patch release of an editor: bump the version number, review candidate fixes, confirm cherry-picked fixes reach the release branch, and prepare release notes describing what changed. Each candidate fix needs a release manager's approval before inclusion, expecting a clean release build once every item is complete.

This is a tracking placeholder for writing the release notes covering a feature that was already stabilized and approved through the normal review process. The notes text still needs to be drafted, including choosing the right category and a short description of the change, with an approval step before it's finalized.

This tracks writing the release-notes text for an already-merged compiler change that shallow-resolves type and const inference variables to their root variables. Someone needs to draft a short description of what changed and pick the right release-notes category, noting whether a compatibility notes section applies. The change itself is already settled; this is just the writeup.

This tracks writing the release-notes entry for a change promoting five embedded, Thumb-instruction-mode Arm compilation targets to a higher support tier. The entry needs the right category and a concise description, and should consider whether a compatibility note or a prominent callout is warranted. Draft the release-notes text summarizing this target-tier promotion.

Tracks writing the release-notes text for a previously merged change that introduces a new compilation target for a pointer-authentication testing variant of a 64-bit ARM Linux platform. Asks the original authors to draft a concise description of the change and decide whether it needs an additional compatibility-notes section.

Manually verify the compact presentation of a sessions list and its empty-group filtering by exercising ordinary session-management workflows from start to finish. Configure a window with several sessions in different states, including at least one completed, one active, and one waiting for input, and confirm the compact and grouped views behave correctly.

Provide a manual test plan for a new, experimental rendering style for progress indicators shown persistently in a chat interface, asking testers to exercise it during their regular day-to-day use across operating systems and confirm it behaves and renders as intended.

This is a manual verification checklist for a recent security hardening change to an agent tool that creates and runs tasks. It needs someone to confirm: a label matching an existing task doesn't bypass confirmation, modify the tasks file, or run anything; a workspace folder outside the current session is rejected before any file access; and even in auto-approve or autopilot modes, explicit confirmation is still required before the tool runs.

This is a manual test-plan item to verify the F2 inline-rename behavior for rows in the agent window's sessions list. Focus a session row, press F2, confirm inline rename starts for that row, accepts a valid title, and correctly restores focus afterward. Walk through each step and confirm the expected behavior holds before this release ships.

This is a manual test-plan item tied to a couple of already-merged changes. Steps: open a chat session with multiple conversations, switch the display setting from a single combined view to multiple tabs via the session header menu, then verify every open conversation gets its own tab, clicking a tab switches correctly, and the relevant menu item's checked state stays correct. Carry out this verification.

A manual test plan for checking that issue and pull-request references in the editor's chat view get rich previews: open the chat panel in the main editor window rather than the dedicated agent window, sign in, start a new chat, and submit a prompt referencing two issues and two pull requests. Wait for the reference list to populate, then open it and use keyboard navigation to check the previews, including a few follow-up focus checks.

Manually validate that sandboxing for the agent host works correctly in both the main window and the editor window, across Windows, macOS, WSL, and Linux. Install available security updates first, use the latest build with a local workspace that's safe to modify, and confirm sandboxing behaves as expected on each platform.

Provide a manual verification checklist, following a change already merged elsewhere, confirming that opening the keyboard-shortcuts view and the running-extensions view from within an editor's agents-window session both open as modal editors rather than regular tabs.

This is a manual test-plan item asking someone to verify, on Windows, macOS, and Linux, that an agent chat session correctly shows the effective sandbox policy. With the terminal agent sandbox disabled, start a new session, confirm a specific slash command appears in autocomplete, run it, and check that it completes and reports the expected sandbox state for that platform.

On Windows, watching a directory non-recursively and then deleting it makes the watcher start emitting rename events for the watched path at an extreme rate — around 190,000 a second — and it never stops, even after a directory with the same name is recreated. It should instead report a permission error when the watched directory is removed. I have a minimal script that reliably triggers this.

Compiling code where a closure captures a value without a statically known size, inside an iterator-mapping call, crashes the compiler internally instead of showing a type error. A reproduction, compiler version, and error output are attached; the cause looks like an internal function computing captured-variable types running before those types are inferred. Fix the ordering so this yields a normal diagnostic, not a crash.

When resolving a module inside a dependency that provides a directory containing an index declaration file, calling the module-resolution API directly only populates the resulting package-identity field when resolving the specific index file path, not when resolving the containing directory path, even though both resolve to the same underlying file. A small reproduction package demonstrating both resolution calls side by side is available.

A hook that restates an implementation guideline has no file-pattern condition, so it fires on every write or edit rather than only on source files, unlike two similar hooks beside it that are correctly scoped. Editing a Markdown, YAML, or scratch file triggers an irrelevant reminder alongside the one that actually applies; it should be scoped the same way the other two hooks are.

Report that a TLS connection ends with a bad record mac error when an HTTPS response passes through a backpressure-applying compression stream over an HTTP CONNECT proxy, and report that the root cause is an extra TLS record the proxy stack injects, not a defect in TLS, streaming, or compression. Reproduce with a large response body compressed over a proxied connection.

Validating a particular tool from an MCP extension fails with an error saying its parameter schema is missing a required items definition on an array-typed parameter, which stops the tool from being usable. The error message points people to file the issue against whichever MCP server or extension provides that tool, rather than the editor itself. A specific editor build, OS version, and hardware details are included in the report.

Running a sizeable App Router production build with the newer bundler engine, where many CSS files pass through PostCSS (via a Tailwind plugin, say) and the project has a CommonJS PostCSS config file, the build fails evaluating that config with an internal error about a context function not being callable. A minimal app rarely triggers it - mostly shows up on large builds - but a reproduction exists.

On a specific recent release line of an automation tool's engine, when a play sets its connection plugin using its short, unqualified name, a magic variable reporting the active connection shows the short name on the first loop iteration but the fully qualified name on every later iteration, with nothing in the playbook changing it. The same playbook doesn't show this on the prior release line. Investigate and restore the prior behavior.

Rework the plugin system end to end: a new loading model, sandboxed execution, a versioned plugin API and a migration path for every existing plugin. That is far too large for one change, so set a direction first and split it into child items.

Offer the whole command line in a second language: translated messages, localised help, locale-aware number formats and a translation workflow for contributors. Plan how to break this into pieces we can land separately.
Move the project from callbacks to promises everywhere, in the core, the adapters and the examples, without stranding existing users. We need a direction and a staged plan of separate changes.
